plotting_plan.title: Three Paradigms for Constraint Satisfaction Reasoning on Sudoku-Extreme
plotting_plan.objective: Conceptual architecture diagram contrasting the three evaluated solver paradigms: (a) direct LLM autoregressive reasoning via chain-of-thought tokens, (b) LLM-synthesized deterministic standard-library backtracking Python solvers, and (c) classical Hopfield-style energy minimization (CRAM) trained via pseudolikelihood and solved via focused Gibbs search.

plotting_plan.title: Inference Latency vs. Cost per Puzzle across Paradigms
plotting_plan.objective: Scatter plot (log-log scale) illustrating the trade-off between median inference latency (milliseconds to seconds) and monetary cost per puzzle (USD) across direct LLM prompting (Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, Haiku 5.5), LLM-synthesized code execution, and CRAM energy minimization.

plotting_plan.title: Recovered Pairwise Couplings vs. Ground-Truth Sudoku Constraints
plotting_plan.objective: Heatmap visualization showing the top-20 learned same-digit coupling weights across all 81 cells compared to the ground-truth Sudoku constraint graph (row, column, and 3x3 box peers), demonstrating 1.000 peer recovery.

introduction_strategy.hook_hypothesis: Recent benchmark results on hard constraint-satisfaction tasks such as Sudoku-Extreme have motivated claims that recurrent neural networks and classical energy-based models learn genuine algorithmic reasoning.
introduction_strategy.problem_gap_hypothesis: The relative cost, wall-clock efficiency, and reliability of energy-based reasoning models, direct frontier LLM chain-of-thought generation, and LLM-synthesized deterministic solvers have not been systematically evaluated under an identical hardware budget and test distribution.

related_work_strategy.overview: Examine three methodology clusters in constraint solving and reasoning: energy-based recurrent models, direct LLM chain-of-thought reasoning, and LLM code generation for algorithmic tasks.

subsections.bridge_to_our_method: We benchmark zero-shot standard-library Python backtracking solvers written by LLMs across all 500 Sudoku-Extreme test puzzles on cost, execution speed, and accuracy.

content_bullets: Contextualize the debate on whether looped models or classical energies learn algorithmic reasoning on combinatorial benchmarks such as Sudoku-Extreme.

Formulate the comparative hypothesis evaluating three distinct paradigm families on identical puzzles under a strict low-cost CPU hardware budget: direct LLM reasoning, LLM-generated Python solvers, and classical Hopfield-style energy minimization (CRAM).

Summarize the key experimental findings: direct LLM reasoning (Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, Haiku 5.5) is slow (105-166 s median), expensive ($0.014-$0.426 per puzzle), and prone to context exhaustion; prompting the same LLMs to write Python backtracking solvers yields 100% accuracy (4,500/4,500 puzzle runs) at 1.0-1.8 ms per puzzle for pennies in code generation cost; an independent CPU re-implementation of CRAM solves 496-497/500 puzzles in 53-61 ms, matching a hand-set single-weight baseline (497/500).
Conclude that Sudoku-Extreme does not sufficiently prove emergent algorithmic reasoning, and code synthesis represents the most cost-effective and reliable deployment path.

subsections.subsection_title: 1.1 The Reasoning Debate: Energy Models vs. Foundation Models
content_bullets: Introduce the rise of constraint-satisfaction benchmarks such as Sudoku-Extreme to substantiate claims of emergent reasoning in neural and energy architectures.
Discuss the recent proposal of CRAM (Hoover et al., 2026), which reports 99.996% accuracy with sub-second GPU training, contrasting with frontier LLM direct chain-of-thought approaches.
Establish the necessity of an apples-to-apples, hardware-constrained benchmark across speed, monetary cost, and algorithmic fidelity.
Independent CPU Replication of CRAM: Provide an independent NumPy/C implementation of classical Hopfield-style energy training and focused Gibbs search without proprietary GPU acceleration.
Direct LLM Evaluation: Quantify token consumption, monetary expense, and error profiles of Claude 5.5 (Opus, Sonnet, Haiku) performing direct chain-of-thought puzzle solving.
Programmatic Delegation Paradigm: Demonstrate that one-shot prompt-generated Python backtracking solvers achieve 100% solve rates at millisecond speeds.

Constraint Recovery and Expressivity Analysis: Prove that learned CRAM couplings reproduce the exact Sudoku constraint graph (peer recovery = 1.000), but perform identically to an unlearned single-parameter energy.

subsections.subsection_title: 2.1 Classical Energy Models and Neural Constraint Satisfaction
content_bullets: Review Hopfield-Tank continuous energy formulations and discrete Ising/Boltzmann machines for combinatorial search.
Detail modern energy-based architectures and pseudolikelihood estimation over discrete graphical models.
Contextualize CRAM's claim of outperforming recurrent neural models by orders of magnitude.
Discuss frontier LLMs with adaptive test-time compute, reasoning tokens, and chain-of-thought prompting.
Examine programmatic reasoning, neuro-symbolic delegation, and program-aided language models that replace autoregressive rollouts with executable code.
Formalize the direct prompt formulation on Sudoku-Extreme boards using adaptive thinking with effort set to high.
Specify the output token budget capped at 32,000 tokens per instance.
Define logging criteria for token-exhaustion failures, incorrect terminal boards, and wall-clock execution times.
Specify the zero-shot prompt instructing frontier LLMs to output self-contained, standard-library Python Sudoku solvers.
Explain the generation protocol: generating 3 independent solvers per model (Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, Haiku 5.5) yielding 9 solvers total.
Formalize the execution pipeline running each synthesized solver across the complete 500-puzzle test split.

subsections.subsection_title: 3.3 Paradigm 3: Independent CRAM Energy Formulation and Inference
content_bullets: Formalize the energy function $E(\mathbf{X})$ over the $81 \times 9$ discrete belief grid: negative entropy term, pairwise $9 \times 9$ cell coupling matrices $\mathbf{W}_{i,j}$, and unary bias vectors $\mathbf{b}_i$.
Detail the pseudolikelihood parameter estimation in NumPy over 1,000 solved training boards without giving the model row, column, or box coordinates (cells treated as opaque indices).
Formulate the focused Gibbs search algorithm implemented in C: executing 4 parallel chains initialized from random boards on a single CPU core with a 10-million move budget.
Define the hand-set energy baseline using Hopfield-Tank penalty rules governed by a single uniform weight without training.
Describe the evaluation dataset: sapientinc/sudoku-extreme, 500 test puzzles drawn from 5 seeded random pages with a median of 26 clues per puzzle.
Detail the training partition for CRAM: first 1,000 solved boards of the training split.
Report the execution environment: single Apple M4 Pro laptop CPU, no GPU acceleration, with total LLM API budget capped at $3.75.
Define evaluation metrics: solved rate, wrong-answer rate, token exhaustion rate, median/p90 latency, API dollar cost per puzzle and per solved puzzle, and constraint graph peer recovery score.

subsections.subsection_title: 4.2 Direct LLM Reasoning Performance and Failure Modes
content_bullets: Analyze direct solving results: Opus 5.5 (3/5 solved, median 124.9 s, $0.426/puzzle), Sonnet 5.5 (3/5 solved, median 166.1 s, $0.250/puzzle), and Haiku 5.5 (3/10 solved, median 105.7 s, $0.014/puzzle).
Examine token exhaustion failures: Sonnet and Opus both exhausted the 32,000 token limit on the exact same two hard puzzles (difficulty ratings 88 and 15).
Document catastrophic hallucination in Haiku 5.5: 2 wrong answers output as final completions with 74/81 and 78/81 cells correct.

subsections.subsection_title: 4.3 Synthesized Programmatic Solvers: Efficiency and Accuracy
content_bullets: Report programmatic solver evaluation: 9 out of 9 synthesized solvers solved all 500 puzzles perfectly (4,500/4,500 successful runs).
Highlight runtime speed: median per-puzzle latency of 1.02-1.48 ms (Sonnet), 1.14-1.85 ms (Haiku), and 1.19-1.66 ms (Opus), processing 500 puzzles in under 1.8 seconds.
Compare synthesis cost: $0.003-$0.005 (Haiku), $0.018-$0.020 (Sonnet), $0.051-$0.063 (Opus) across 96-128 lines of standard-library Python code written in 12-44 seconds.

subsections.subsection_title: 4.4 CRAM Replication, Constraint Recovery, and Baseline Equivalence
content_bullets: Evaluate learned CRAM across 3 training seeds: 496-497/500 solved puzzles, 0 wrong stops, median latency of 53.2-61.1 ms (p90 351-425 ms), fit time of 2.51-2.52 seconds on CPU.
Evaluate hand-set single-weight baseline: solves 497/500 puzzles with 0 fit time, median latency 42.8 ms (p90 311 ms), perfectly matching or exceeding learned CRAM.
Examine constraint graph recovery: learned same-digit couplings achieve 1.000 peer recovery, placing true row/column/box peers in the top-20 weights for all 81 cells.

Verify direct comparison on LLM subsets: learned CRAM solves 10/10 LLM test puzzles (0.3 ms to 1.29 s), including the two instances that triggered token exhaustion in Opus and Sonnet (66 ms and 122 ms).

subsections.subsection_title: 5.1 Summary of Findings and Implications for Reasoning Benchmarks
content_bullets: Synthesize comparative findings across LLM direct thinking, LLM code generation, and classical energy optimization.
Reiterate that delegating constraint satisfaction to synthesized code is 5 orders of magnitude faster and 100x cheaper than direct autoregression.

Discuss the theoretical implication: because an unlearned single-weight energy matches learned CRAM, Sudoku-Extreme primarily benchmarks local consistency search rather than complex abstract reasoning.
Acknowledge the small sample size (5-10 puzzles per model) for direct LLM solving necessitated by extreme API token consumption.
Clarify that original CRAM 42 ms GPU training benchmarks are from Hoover et al., whereas our replication focuses on single-core CPU execution.
Propose future directions on non-local constraint problems where single-weight energy landscapes provably fail.
State full reproducibility parameters: exact Hugging Face dataset split, pseudorandom seeds (0, 1, 2), prompt text, and single-CPU execution environment.
Document availability of C focused Gibbs search source code and Python driver scripts.
